title: Reading the Dog class and method overrides with a base class
reading_goal: Read the code to determine which implementation is selected when a method with the same name in a subclass is called in conjunction with the base class notation.
question: What is the direct reason that `pet.speak()` returns `bark`?
choices: Since `Animal` does not have a `speak()` method,
explanation: `Dog(Animal)` establishes an inheritance relationship, and the Dog class redefines `speak()`. Since `pet` is a Dog instance, `pet.speak()` uses Dog’s method to return `bark`. This is because when a subclass overrides a method with the same name as its parent, that implementation is selected when the subclass instance is called. A common source of confusion: Since Animal does not have a `speak()` method, the subclass also has `speak()` and returns `sound`. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the body of the parent class is not examined. Inheritance code follows this sequence: **check the base class → check for overriding → select the implementation that matches the instance type**.
project_context: This ties into understanding the differences in behavior between base classes and subclasses in class-based app and server code, as well as in libraries.
reading_goal_internal: base class 표기와 subclass 내부의 같은 이름 메서드를 연결해 호출 시 어떤 구현이 선택되는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `class Child(Base):` This is a class definition where ``Child`` inherits from ``Base``.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: After checking the base class in parentheses, see if a method with the same name is redefined in the subclass body.
concept_explanation.key_point: Although Dog inherits from Animal, it directly redefines `speak()`, so Dog instances use Dog’s implementation.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the parent method is always executed because it’s inherited. However, if a subclass overrides the same method, its implementation takes precedence.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Although `Bike` inherits from `Vehicle`, it overrides `kind()`, so `bike` is printed.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `Dog(Animal)` It establishes an inheritance relationship, and the Dog class redefines ``speak()``. Since ``pet`` is a Dog instance, ``pet.speak()`` uses Dog’s methods to return ``bark``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because when a subclass overrides a method with the same name as its parent, that implementation is selected when the subclass instance is called.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Since `Animal` does not have a `speak()` method,
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The `Animal` class also has a ``speak()`` method and returns a ``sound``.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the body of the parent class has not been checked.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Inheritance code is read as **check the base class → check if it is overridden → select the implementation that matches the instance type**.

title: Understanding the structure where `@property` is applied to the method immediately below it
reading_goal: Read about the relationship between function decorators and decorated methods, and understand why the calculated value is accessed without parentheses.
question: `cfg.is_fast` Why does the calculation produce a result even when read without parentheses?
explanation: `@property` turns the `is_fast` method immediately below it into a property. Therefore, accessing the `cfg.is_fast` property triggers the execution of the internal function, and since the current mode is `fast`, it returns `True`. This is because the property decorator allows a method to be used as a descriptor-based property. Common misconception: Since `print` automatically calls the method, it simply outputs the passed value and does not perform property conversion. Point of Misinterpretation: This is a case where the role of the decorator was mistakenly attributed to `print`. Note that a decorator **is applied to the definition immediately below it and can subsequently change how it is used**.
project_context: This relates to reading code that exposes values calculated from configuration objects or model objects as if they were regular attributes.
reading_goal_internal: function decorator와 decorated method의 관계를 읽고 호출 괄호 없이 계산된 값을 접근하는 이유를 이해한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A function decorator is a syntax where `@name` is written immediately above a function definition to wrap or transform that definition with different behavior.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Treat the decorator line and the `def` immediately below it as a pair, and observe how their usage changes afterward.
concept_explanation.key_point: `@property` `is_fast`, when applied, reads values from an instance in the form of attribute access, such as ``cfg.is_fast``.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that `cfg.is_fast()` must be called. The `property` executes an internal getter when the attribute is accessed.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `status` is a property, reading it as `user.status` will output `on`, which is the result of an internal calculation.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `@property` This creates the ``is_fast`` method as a property. Therefore, accessing the attribute ``cfg.is_fast`` triggers the execution of the internal function, and since the current mode is `fast`, it returns `True`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because a property decorator allows methods to be accessed as descriptor-based attributes.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `print` simply outputs the values passed to it; it does not perform property conversion.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the role of a decorator was mistakenly described as that of `print`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read that a **decorator is applied to the definition immediately below it and can be used differently afterward**.

title: Read the execution flow where a function decorator applies a wrapper.
reading_goal: A decorator returns a wrapper when defining a function and tracks the flow so that subsequent calls begin with the wrapper.
question: In the final `run()` call, what is printed before `run`?
explanation: `@log_call` When applied, ``log_call`` returns ``wrapper``. Subsequent calls to ``run()`` execute the `wrapper`, which first outputs ``before`` and then calls the original `run`. This is because the function returned by the decorator is bound to the name of the decorated function. A common source of confusion: The original `run` is called later within the `wrapper` at ``fn()``. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when you overlook the fact that the target of the call is the wrapper after the decorator has been applied. The wrapper decorator follows this sequence: **wrapping at definition → wrapper execution begins upon call → original function call**.
project_context: This ties into the fundamentals of reading code from decorator-based libraries, such as FastAPI routes, click commands, and testing tools.
reading_goal_internal: decorator가 함수 정의 시 wrapper를 반환하고 이후 호출이 wrapper부터 시작되는 흐름을 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `@decorator` is a syntax that passes the function definition immediately below it to the decorator, thereby associating the transformed function object with that name.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, look at what the decorator function returns, and then track which function actually starts when the decorated function is called.
concept_explanation.key_point: `log_call` Since it returns ``wrapper``, the subsequent ``run()`` begins with the wrapper behavior.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think that a decorator is redefined every time `run()` is called. However, the decorator is applied when the function is defined, and when the function is called, the wrapped function is executed.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the `decorator` returns `wrapped`, when it is called, `trace` is printed first, followed by the original `save` function.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `@log_call` When applied, ``log_call`` returns ``wrapper``. Subsequently, the call to ``run()`` executes the wrapper, which first prints ``before`` and then calls the original `run`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the function returned by the decorator is associated with the name of the decorated function.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Originally, `run` is called later within the `fn()` function in the wrapper.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where the learner failed to recognize that the target of the call is `wrapper` after the decorator was applied.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A wrapper decorator is interpreted in the following order: **wrapping upon definition → wrapper execution upon call → call to the original function**.

title: Understanding the Execution Order of `with` in a Custom Context Manager
reading_goal: Track the order in which the `with` statement executes the context manager’s entry, body, and exit operations.
question: Which of the following is closest to the order of output?
explanation: When entering `with Timer():`, `__enter__()` runs first and prints `start`. The body then prints `work`, and when leaving the block, `__exit__()` prints `end`. This is because the context-manager protocol calls entry and exit hooks before and after the `with` block. Common wrong answer: `work → start → end`. Context entry happens before the body. Misreading point: This happens when the entry step of the `with` statement is skipped. Read `with` in the order **enter → body → exit**.
project_context: It relates to code that safely handles resources—such as files, database connections, locks, and sessions—which require cleanup before and after use.
reading_goal_internal: with statement가 context manager 진입·본문·종료 동작을 어떤 순서로 실행하는지 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `with manager:` is a statement that executes its body between the entry and exit of a context manager.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Execute the actions performed upon entry, followed by the indented body, and then the actions performed upon block exit.
concept_explanation.key_point: In a custom context manager, ``__enter__`` typically handles the behavior at the start, and ``__exit__`` handles the behavior at the end.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that the body is executed first and `__enter__` comes later. However, the entry handling occurs before the body.

teaching_example.walkthrough: It is printed in the following order: “open” at the entry point, “use” in the body, and “close” at the exit point.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: When entering `with Timer():`, `__enter__()` runs first and prints “start.” Next, the main body prints “work,” and upon exiting, `__exit__()` prints “end.”
answer_explanation.why_correct: Because the context-manager protocol calls entry and exit hooks before and after the `with` block.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Context initialization occurs before the main text.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the entry point of the `with` statement was skipped.

answer_explanation.takeaway: "with" is read in the order **enter → body → exit**.

title: Tracking from `asyncio.run(main())` to the `await` result
reading_goal: Track the asynchronous execution flow starting from `asyncio.run` through the `await` in `main` to the `fetch` return.
code:
import asyncio

async def fetch():
    return "data"

async def main():
    result = await fetch()
    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())
question: What is the output?
explanation: The `main` coroutine is executed, and since the result of ``await fetch()`` is ``data``, `result` becomes `data`. The `print` statement then outputs that value because the actual output target is `result`, which stores the return value of `fetch`. A common source of confusion: “main” is just the name of a function; it is not the value that `print` outputs. Common Misinterpretation: This occurs when the name of the called function is confused with the data flow inside the function. For async output, trace the flow as **entry call → await → return value → usage location**.
project_context: It relates to reading the entry point and `await` flow in code that calls asynchronous API servers, crawlers, and agent tools.
reading_goal_internal: asyncio.run에서 시작해 main의 await와 fetch return까지 이어지는 비동기 실행 흐름을 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `asyncio.run(coro)` is a top-level asyncio helper function call used to execute a coroutine.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It identifies which async function created the coroutine passed in parentheses and follows it all the way to the inner `await`.
concept_explanation.key_point: The output value is determined not by the name of `asyncio.run` itself, but by the actual return value of the `fetch` function awaited within `main`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that async functions execute automatically simply by being defined.

teaching_example.code:
import asyncio

async def value():
    return 3

async def main():
    result = await value()
    print(result)

asyncio.run(main())
teaching_example.walkthrough: `value` returns 3, and `main` awaits this value and then prints 3.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since the `main` coroutine is executed and the result of `await fetch()` is `data`, `result` becomes `data`. The `print` statement then outputs that value.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the actual output destination is `result`, which stores the return value of `fetch`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `main` is only a function name; it is not the value printed by `print`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of confusion between the name of the called object and the data flow within the function.

answer_explanation.takeaway: We also trace async output using the sequence **entry call → await → return value → usage location**.

title: Waiting for an asynchronous HTTP response with `await client.get()`
reading_goal: Read the structure where the `await` statement is used to receive the `response` object upon completion of the `async HTTP client` method.
question: What is `await client.get(...)` waiting for?
explanation: `client.get` creates an async task representing an HTTP request, and `await` waits until that task completes and returns a `Response` object. This is because the result of an async HTTP GET is a `Response`. A common source of confusion: CSS rendering code does not contain CSS processing logic. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the role of the HTTP client is confused with UI rendering. Asynchronous HTTP code should be read as **request call → await → response object**.
project_context: This relates to the basic flow of handling bulk API calls or internal asynchronous requests in FastAPI.
reading_goal_internal: async HTTP client method의 완료 결과를 await해 response 객체를 받는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `await expression` is an expression that waits for an awaitable operation to complete and then receives its result.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check what the right-hand side of the `await` call does and where the return value is stored after it completes.
concept_explanation.key_point: In an async get call from an HTTP client, you must await until the network I/O is complete and the response is received.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to think `await` waits for the URL string itself. It waits for the asynchronous work created by the `get` call.

teaching_example.walkthrough: When the async result of `get` completes, it returns a `response` dictionary and returns status code 201.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `client.get` creates an async task representing an HTTP request, and `await` waits until that task completes and returns a `Response` object.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the result of an async HTTP GET is a `response`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The code does not contain any CSS processing logic.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of confusing the role of an HTTP client with UI rendering.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Asynchronous HTTP code follows the pattern: **request call → await → response object**.

title: Reading the `body.text` attribute of the requested model instance
reading_goal: Understand the structure in which the model instance reads `field` as an instance attribute representing the request body.
question: What value is stored in `question`?
explanation: `Question("RAG란?")` When the object is created, a string is stored in ``self.text``. Later, ``body.text`` reads that attribute and assigns it to ``question``, because instance attribute access returns the value of the attribute stored in that object. Common source of confusion: “text`text`” is the attribute name, while the actual stored value is “`RAG란?`.” Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the attribute name and the attribute value are confused. The model object interprets the process as **check instance → check attribute name → read stored value**.
project_context: In the learning app’s question API or RAG query API, the request body is verified as a model object before being routed to the server code that reads the fields.
reading_goal_internal: 요청 본문을 나타내는 모델 인스턴스에서 field를 instance attribute로 읽는 구조를 이해한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `object.name` is an expression that reads an attribute associated with an instance.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check what the object on the left is, and find the value of the attribute on the right stored in that instance.
concept_explanation.key_point: In the context of FastAPI/Pydantic, the request body is prepared as a model instance, and fields can be read as `body.text`. The sample code fixes this as a local object to verify only Python’s native behavior.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `body.text` It’s easy to mistake this for a dict key lookup. However, since it uses dot notation rather than square brackets, it’s attribute access.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The `content` attribute of the `Message` instance’s body is read, and `hello` is stored in `value`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `Question("RAG란?")` When generated, the string is stored in ``self.text``. Subsequently, ``body.text`` reads that attribute and assigns it to ``question``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Because instance attribute access returns the attribute value stored on that object.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: `text` is the attribute name, and the actual stored value is `RAG란?`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an instance where the attribute name and attribute value were confused.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The model interprets the object as **check instance → check attribute name → read stored value**.

title: Reading the `status_code` keyword argument of the `route` decorator
reading_goal: Within a decorator call, read the keyword argument names and values separately and associate them with the route response settings.
question: In `status_code=200`, what value is `200` passed as?
explanation: `status_code=200` is a keyword argument inside the `app.get()` call, so 200 is the setting value passed under the name `status_code`. In Python call syntax, `name=value` passes a value to the parameter with that name. A tempting wrong answer is `DB id`, but this code configures a route decorator rather than reading a database ID. Read `name=value` inside a call as a **setting name and supplied value pair**.
project_context: It is linked to a code review that configures the API server response status in the route declaration and tracks client errors.
reading_goal_internal: decorator 호출 안에서 keyword argument 이름과 값을 분리해 읽고 route 응답 설정과 연결한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `name=value` Values passed to a call in this format are keyword arguments.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check what the name on the left refers to and read the actual value on the right.
concept_explanation.key_point: `status_code=200` is a route configuration value passed to the `app.get()` call, not an iteration count or a DB ID.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to mistake 200 for the function’s return value. The 200 at this location is the value of an argument passed to the call.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `code=202` is a named keyword argument, the value 202 is passed to the `code` parameter.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `status_code=200``app.get()` is a keyword argument within the `` call. Therefore, 200 is a configuration value passed under the name ``status_code``.
answer_explanation.why_correct: In Python call syntax, `name=value` is a keyword argument that passes a value to the corresponding parameter name.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This is not code that reads a DB ID; it is a route decorator configuration.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the calling context surrounding the number 200 was not checked.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The ``name=value`` function reads **configuration names and their corresponding values as pairs**.

title: Reading the list literal passed to CORS `allow_origins`
reading_goal: The keyword argument reads the items in the list literal on the right to interpret the list of allowed sources.
code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://example.com"],
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST"],
)
question: `allow_origins` How many sources are passed to it?
explanation: `allow_origins` The list on the right contains only one string. Therefore, there is only one source being passed. This is because the number of items in a list literal is determined by the number of values actually written inside the square brackets. A common source of confusion: Instead of a wildcard string like ``*``, which would mean “all sources,” a specific URL is written here. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when you focus only on the CORS concept without verifying the actual list values. For the configuration list, **count the actual items, verify the values, and then connect them to their domain meanings**.
project_context: This relates to security and web settings that restrict allowed origins when connecting a front end, such as GitHub Pages, to a separate API server.
reading_goal_internal: keyword argument 오른쪽 list literal의 항목을 읽어 허용 출처 목록을 해석한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `[value1, value2]` is a list literal that directly creates a sequence of values.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the number and values of the items inside the square brackets, then see where that list is passed.
concept_explanation.key_point: Here, a list containing a single URL string is passed to `allow_origins`.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that because square brackets are used, all sources are automatically allowed. In reality, you should only read the items explicitly listed in the list.

teaching_example.code: allowed_hosts = ["https://app.example", "https://admin.example"]
teaching_example.walkthrough: The list contains two strings in order and represents the allowlist as data.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `allow_origins` The list on the right contains only one string. Therefore, there is also only one source being passed.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the number of items in a list literal is determined by the number of values actually written inside the square brackets.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Instead of a wildcard string `*`, which represents all sources, a single specific URL is listed.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case of considering only the CORS concept without checking the actual list values.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The configuration list **counts the actual items, verifies their values, and then connects them to their domain meanings**.

title: Reading the call to the SQLite conn.commit() method
reading_goal: Read that calling the `commit` method of the `connection` object after an `INSERT` operation is the step that finalizes transaction changes.
code:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE notes(title TEXT, body TEXT)")
conn.execute(
    "INSERT INTO notes(title, body) VALUES (?, ?)",
    ("memo", "hello"),
)
conn.commit()
question: `conn.commit()` Which of the following best describes its role?
explanation: After an INSERT operation makes changes to the connection, `conn.commit()` is called. Commit finalizes the changes made by that transaction. This is because the commit method of a DB connection is the step that permanently reflects the changes from the pending transaction. Common Confusion: This is a call to a DB connection method, not a file I/O function for reading a file. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the receiver `conn` and the preceding SQL context are not verified. To understand the save flow, you must read the DB code all the way through **executing changes → checking whether to commit**.
project_context: It is linked to the transaction flow of the server code that stores notes, progress, and curation results in the database.
reading_goal_internal: INSERT 실행 이후 connection 객체의 commit 메서드 호출이 transaction 변경을 확정하는 단계임을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `object.method()` calls a method belonging to a specific object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the object and method names to the left of the dot, and see how that call handles the state created by the preceding code.
concept_explanation.key_point: `conn.commit()` is not a call that creates a new INSERT, but rather a step that commits database changes that have already been made.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `execute()` Since it’s there, it’s easy to think of a commit as a simple query. Here, however, it’s the process of finalizing an INSERT change.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The receiver is `session`, and the called method is `commit`. The return value is `saved`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: After INSERT makes changes to the connection, `conn.commit()` is called. commit finalizes the changes made by that transaction.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the `commit` method of a database connection is the step that permanently applies changes made by a pending transaction.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This is a call to a database connection method, not a file I/O function.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the receiver `conn` and the preceding SQL context were not checked.

answer_explanation.takeaway: To understand the save flow, you must read the DB code up to the point of **executing the changes → checking whether to commit**.

title: Read the parameter-tuple argument of SQL `execute()`.
reading_goal: Note that the second positional argument of the `execute` call is a tuple of values corresponding to SQL placeholders.
code:
query = "SELECT * FROM items WHERE source = ?"
source_name = "manual"
rows = conn.execute(query, (source_name,)).fetchall()
question: What is the value of the second positional argument in `conn.execute()`?
choices: source_name A tuple containing a single item
answer: source_name A tuple containing a single item
explanation: `execute(query, (source_name,))` The first argument is `query`, and the second is ``(source_name,)``. Due to the trailing comma, the second argument is a one-element tuple. In Python, ``(value,)`` is a one-element tuple, and this value is passed as the second positional argument to `execute`. A common source of confusion: the SQL string itself. The SQL string is the first argument, ``query``. Point of Misinterpretation: This occurs when the order of the two positional arguments is not distinguished. Parameter-binding code checks whether **the SQL statement and the tuple of values are passed as separate arguments**.
project_context: This relates to secure server code that passes user and collected data values via parameter binding rather than concatenating them directly into an SQL string.
reading_goal_internal: execute 호출의 두 번째 positional argument가 SQL placeholder에 대응할 값들의 tuple이라는 점을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: Expressions passed in order without names within parentheses are called positional arguments.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Count the arguments from the left and verify the actual type and value of each expression.
concept_explanation.key_point: The comma in `(source_name,)` indicates that this is a single-element tuple and is passed separately from the query string.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that just because there are parentheses, it’s a simple string. For a tuple, the trailing comma is key.

teaching_example.code:
def execute(query, params):
    return params

name = "sensor"
params = execute("SELECT ... WHERE name = ?", (name,))
teaching_example.walkthrough: The second positional argument is the one-item tuple `("sensor",)`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: `execute(query, (source_name,))` The first argument is `query`, and the second is ``(source_name,)``. Because of the trailing comma, the second argument is a tuple containing a single item.
answer_explanation.why_correct: In Python, ``(value,)`` is a single-element tuple, and this value is passed as the second positional argument to `execute`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The SQL string is the first argument, `query`.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the order of the two positional arguments was not distinguished.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The parameter binding code checks **whether the SQL statement and the value tuple are passed as separate arguments**.

title: Concatenating two DataFrames using the `pd.concat()` return value
reading_goal: Understand the flow of values where the list of DataFrames passed as inputs to the `pd.concat` call and the resulting DataFrame are stored in `combined`.
code:
import pandas as pd
df_old = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})
df_new = pd.DataFrame({"id": [3, 4]})
combined = pd.concat([df_old, df_new], ignore_index=True)
print(len(combined))
question: What value does `len(combined)` return after the `concat` call?
explanation: The second row of `df_old` and the second row of `df_new` are passed to the `concat` call. Since the default `axis=0`, the rows are concatenated to return a 4-row DataFrame, which is stored in `combined`. This is because the total number of rows in the two inputs is 2+2. A common source of confusion: This result is based on looking at only the number of rows in one DataFrame. `concat` combines both inputs. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the argument list of the call is not checked all the way through. title: Reading x + y Broadcasting Addition in NumPy Arrays
reading_goal: In the arithmetic expression `x + y`, read the process by which NumPy’s shape compatibility rules map `y` to each row to compute the element-wise sum.
code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
y = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(x + y)
question: What is the result of ``x + y`` with broadcasting applied?
explanation: The length of each row in x and the length of y are both 3. The three values of y are added element-by-element to the first and second rows, respectively, to produce the two result rows. This is because, in NumPy broadcasting, the (3,) vector is compatible with the last dimension of the (2,3) array. A common source of confusion: [11, 22, 33]—this contains only the result for the first row. The same y is applied to the second row as well. Common Misinterpretation: This occurs when the process is calculated as if broadcasting were applied only once to the entire row. When working with array arithmetic, do not focus solely on the operators; also consider the shapes of each operand and the corresponding rules.
project_context: This connects to reading shape-based broadcasting results when arrays and vectors are operated on together in model-input, embedding, or normalization code.
reading_goal_internal: `x + y` arithmetic expression에서 NumPy의 shape 호환 규칙이 y를 각 행에 대응시켜 원소별 합을 만드는 과정을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: In Python, the `+` operator performs the addition operation defined by the object. When used with NumPy arrays, element-wise addition and broadcasting rules may apply.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Compare the shapes of the two arrays starting from the rightmost dimension, and if they are compatible, calculate row by row which values correspond and are added together.
concept_explanation.key_point: (2,3) For arrays and (3,) vectors, the last dimension is 3, so y corresponds to each row.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that `y` is added only to the first row. However, if the broadcasting conditions are met, the same three positions correspond to every row.

teaching_example.code:

x = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
y = np.array([10, 20])
print(x + y)
teaching_example.walkthrough: The values 10 and 20 for y correspond to each of the two lines, resulting in [[11,22],[13,24]].

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The length of each row of x and the length of y are both 3. The three values of y are added element-by-element to the first and second rows, respectively, to produce two result rows.
answer_explanation.why_correct: In NumPy broadcasting, the (3,) vector is compatible with the last dimension of the (2,3) array.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This includes only the result for the first line. The same y applies to the second line as well.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is a case where the step in which `broadcasting` is repeatedly applied to the entire row was counted only once.

answer_explanation.takeaway: When studying array arithmetic, don’t just look at the operators; also consider the shape of each operand and the rules governing their interactions.
